title: Concurrency windowing and streaming interaction - architecture review notes
content:
Context:
We ran an architecture review to reconcile two related but often conflicting goals: (1) support low-latency streaming responses for interactive use-cases while (2) maintaining predictable throughput and fair concurrency for multi-tenant hosts. This doc captures the discussion, concrete decisions, and outstanding questions from the 2024-11-07 review.

Attendees:
- Marcus Chen (chair)
- Priya Singh
- Aaron Blum
- Leah Park
- Theo Ramirez
- + engineers from infra and obs (joined for Q&A)

Agenda:
1) Quick problem statement and metrics that surface the problem
2) Proposed designs (slot-window model, soft-preemption, streaming-aware batching)
3) Tradeoffs, failure modes, and observable signals
4) Decision and next steps / owners

Problem statement (short):
Interactive streaming callers (chat UI, tool-calling) produce many long-lived in-flight connections that consume headroom in the inference layer because the model KV cache and prefix state persist across incremental token generation. At high concurrency this collides with our continuous-batching heuristics: either we over-provision slots (wasting GPU memory/throughput) or we under-allocate and see high tail latency and request queuing. Need an architecture that:
- preserves low per-token latency for active streams,
- gives the scheduler enough signal to make fair slot assignments, and
- degrades gracefully when capacity is constrained.

Metrics motivating the work:
- 95th/99th token latency on streaming sessions spikes by 3x when active streaming sessions > 40k across a pool (SRV-3421).
- Memory pressure events correlate with long-lived half-idle streams (client waiting on user typing) accounting for 18% of eviction churn.
- Observed waste: average GPU utilization drops below 60% during heavy interactive tail patterns.

Design proposals considered (high-level):
A. Slot-window model (preferred)
- Each streaming session is assigned a concurrency slot + a sliding "window" budget (N tokens or T seconds) that represents the active generation budget.
- When a session is actively generating within the window, it contributes to continuous batching. When idle but within the window, it keeps a lightweight handle but releases heavy resources (e.g., prefetch slots, KV pinned memory).
- Windows are refreshed on new token generation requests.
- Key idea: separate "active generation" resource from "session affinity" resource.

B. Soft preemption with graceful restart
- When capacity constraint hits, lightly preempt lowest-priority streams by truncating KV prefixes to a compact representation and marking session as "warm" rather than fully hot.
- On next generate, we do a fast warmup path that rebuilds necessary KV state incrementally.
- Accepts extra latency on fallback path but keeps memory utilization bounded.

C. Streaming-aware batching heuristics
- Modify continuous batching to weight queued tokens by estimated completion probability (e.g., partial message length, client typing heuristics) so that short bursts aren't penalized by long-hold streams.
- Use short-window bundling: group tokens for the same session up to a micro-batch size with deadline-based triggers.

D. Client backpressure + hinting (client-side assisted)
- API additions: clients can mark streams as "passive" vs "active"; typing indications; expected token burst size.
- Not acceptable as sole solution (can't trust all clients) but useful as a complementary signal.

Discussion notes and tradeoffs:
- Memory vs Latency: Slot-window model (A) reduces peak memory by converting cold handles to small metadata, but requires fast warmup to avoid client-visible pause. Warmup path complexity was a key concern (Aaron).
- Observability: Must add explicit metrics for window state transitions (hot->warm->cold), warmup time histogram, and warm-up failure rate. Without these signals the scheduler can't make informed decisions.
- Fairness: Soft preemption must consider tenant QoS tiers. We recommended integrating with tenant QoS credits (current design for tenant-qos-credit-routing).
- Complexity: Option B introduces state migration complexity; Option C is an incremental change and lower risk but may not fix the memory blow-up.
- Security: Compacting KV must be verified to not leak other tenant data; Leah flagged additional tests for artifact isolation.

Concrete decisions (consensus):
1) Adopt a hybrid approach: implement the Slot-window model (A) as the canonical runtime change, and prototype Soft preemption (B) only for emergency fallback paths.
2) Streaming-aware batching heuristics (C) will be implemented as incremental improvements to the batching controller; heuristics will be feature-flagged and validated with canaries.
3) Add a small client hint API (D) but treat hints as advisory only; server will ignore hints for untrusted tenants or by default.
4) Observability and SLOs: define warmup latency SLO (p50 < 40ms, p95 < 150ms) for the warmup path and add detailed metrics for window states.

Action items and owners:
- Marcus: write the design RFC for Slot-window model and sequence diagram (due 2024-11-15) (jira:SRV-3499).
- Priya: prototype lightweight session-handle representation and measure memory reduction on a small cluster (due 2024-12-01).
- Aaron: implement warmup fast-path (incremental KV replay) prototype; pair with Priya to validate latency (due 2024-12-08).
- Leah: security/QA checklist for KV compaction + integration tests (due 2024-11-20).
- Theo: update continuous-batching controller to accept session weight heuristic and run A/B on low-traffic pool (feature flag) (due 2024-11-30).
- Observability (assigned to SRE liaison in follow-up): create dashboards and alerting for new metrics (window transitions, warmup latency, warmup failures).

Open questions (needs follow-up):
- How aggressive should the window timeout be for different workload classes? (interactive chat vs streaming TTS) -> propose experiments across tenant QoS tiers.
- What is the cost curve for warmup latency vs memory saved for large models with big KV footprints? (measure with 30B model artifacts)
- Failure semantics: if warmup fails repeatedly, should we tear down session or move to offline transcript? Need product guidance for user-visible behaviour.

Notes to self / rough ideas to capture: (informal)
- Think about a tiny in-memory signature of KV (hash+last-token-index) we can store instead of full cached tensors; can reduce pinned memory significantly.
- Consider a micro-replay API where warmup can be happened lazily while streaming first tokens are being returned (overlap warmup+first-token gen).
- Might reuse the existing prefix-caching eviction hooks but extend them to produce "compact handles" instead of full eviction.

Related tickets / references from meeting:
- SRV-3421 (observed tail latency spikes)
- SRV-3388 (continuous batching heuristics)
- SRV-3499 (new RFC – slot-window design)
- confluence:SRV-Windowing-2024 (working notes)
- github:repo/streaming-kernel-pr#128 (early warmup kernels)

Next meeting / cadence:
- Weekly follow-ups during the prototyping phase. First tech walkthrough of prototype will be scheduled for 2024-12-06.

Appendix: rough slot-window state machine (textual)
- HOT: pinned KV + active slot; receives full resource allocation.
- WARM: compact handle stored, lightweight metadata kept (client routing info, pointer to persistent storage of prefix). Minimal memory.
- COLD: no handle in serving layer; resume requires full restore which is the slowest path.
- Transitions triggered by: inactivity timer, memory pressure signals, tenant QoS eviction.

Slack refs (internal):
- #serving-runtime streaming thread Nov 4 (discussion)
- linked: slack-msg-id: G12345-abcde (client-hint debate)

If you want to try a quick simulation on the harness: recommend running three scenarios (1) 2k hot-concurrent streams for 30s bursts, (2) mix of 10k passive streams with 100 hot bursts, (3) sustained high concurrency with synthetic typing interleaving. Capture warmup histograms and memory delta.

-- end of notes --
